title: Infections of the Nervous, Digestive and Respiratory Systems
lead: The nervous system is not as directly connected to the respiratory and digestive systems as those two are to each other. Most microbial infections of the nervous system arise from bloodborne pathogens, whereas the other two systems are mainly infected by external pathogens that directly contact the organs. However, some respiratory pathogens may enter the bloodstream and then infect the nervous system.

blocks.text: The nervous system is divided into two anatomical divisions: the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS) (Fig. 14.1). CNS includes the brain and the spinal cord; the PNS consists of the nerves, ganglia (masses of nervous tissue containing neuron cell bodies outside the brain and spinal cord), and the sensory receptors (for vision, taste, hearing, balance, and tactile perception).
Fig. 14.1. The nervous system. A. The central nervous system includes the brain and spinal cord. B. The cranium is

shown to highlight the meninges, ventricles, and the flow pathway of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). C. The lower part of the spinal cord is illustrated to show how a sample of CSF (a spinal tap) can be collected by inserting a needle between the lumbar vertebrae in the lower back. D. A diagram of a section of the spinal cord reveals sensory and motor nerves. E. A diagram of a brain section demonstrating the blood-brain barrier, which is formed by numerous astrocyte feet adhering to the blood vessels. Image: Linus Books.

Some components of the CNS and PNS form the autonomic nervous system (ANS), which innervates cardiac muscle, smooth muscle, and glandular epithelia. The autonomic nervous system is not discussed in the chapter. The CNS is in the bony chamber of the cranium and the neural canals of the vertebrae and is protected by three meninges. The dura mater, the outermost of the meninges, is fused to the bones (Fig. 14.1). The middle layer, called the arachnoid mater, is attached by spider web-like processes to the pia mater, the innermost of the three meninges. The pia mater loosely covers the brain and spinal cord. A clear fluid called cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulates in the space between the pia mater and arachnoid mater, as well as in the spaces (ventricles) within the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord (Fig. 14.1). CSF is a watery substance containing a few cells (leukocytes). CSF is normally sterile, but bacteria entering it may grow very rapidly.

The brain is a large sheet of neurons meticulously folded to fit within the cranium. Only a few types of cells make up most of the brain (see Chapter 13). Neurons conduct electrical signals. Oligodendrocytes function like Schwann cells and provide the function of the myelin sheath for axons and dendrites in the brain. Astrocytes cover the blood capillaries in the brain and form the blood-brain barrier (BBB), which quite effectively prevents microbes from entering the brain from the blood. Microglial cells are mobile and may engulf invading microbes and damaged neural tissue. Ependymal cells line the cavities (ventricles) of the brain, and in certain locations, they secrete cerebrospinal fluid. Finally, stellate cells support the ganglia.

The brain is divided into anatomical/functional regions and locations that are not detailed here. The four major regions of the brain are the cerebrum (or forebrain), cerebellum (or hindbrain), pons, and medulla oblongata. The lower end of the medulla oblongata exits the cranial cavity and becomes the spinal cord. The spinal cord is a tube-like organ with a central canal. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flows through the canal and the subarachnoid space. The presence of microbes in CSF can be tested by taking a sample (spinal tap) from the subarachnoid space with a needle puncture between lumbar vertebrae 3 and 4 (Fig. 14.1). Both the brain and spinal cord have regions known as gray matter and white matter (Fig. 14.1). Gray matter is rich in the cell bodies of neurons, while white matter is rich in axons. Many viruses (including poliovirus, rabies virus, herpes simplex virus, and several arboviruses) may infect brain cells in the gray matter, causing encephalitis, a severe brain inflammation.

There are three types of neurons: sensory neurons, motor neurons, and internuncial neurons. The cell body of a motor neuron is located within the brain or spinal cord. Motor neurons transmit signals from the brain to muscles and glands (Fig. 14.2). An internuncial neuron, found in the spinal cord, connects motor and sensory neurons. The cell body of a sensory neuron is typically situated outside the CNS. Sensory neurons carry signals from sensory organs (such as the eyes, tongue, nose, and ears) and tactile receptors in the skin back to the brain. A nerve is a bundle of axons that transports information between the CNS and PNS. Nerves emerging from the brain and medulla oblongata are called cranial nerves, while those emerging from the spinal cord are called spinal nerves. Nerves also contain arteries and veins, and the entire bundle is encased in a matrix and connective tissue membrane (epineurium). Thus, a nerve resembles a sheathed electric wire (Fig. 14.2). A nerve may contain axons of both sensory and motor neurons. We will not discuss sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves, as these are not regular targets of microbial infections.

The neurons transmit electric impulses. The electrophysiology of impulse transmission is beyond the scope of this textbook. Simply put, the electric impulse travels across the cell through the axon. In a naked axon, the impulse travels at about 1 meter per second, but in myelinated axons, it travels over 100 meters per second. The axon of the neuron contacts the dendrite of the next neuron or a muscle or gland through a gap junction called a synapse (Fig. 14.2). When the electrical impulse reaches the synapse, it causes the release of chemical substances called neurotransmitters.

Neurotransmitters are pre-made at the end of the axons and packed in membrane vesicles. The impulse causes specific proteins, known as SNARE proteins, to fuse the vesicles with the plasma membrane. The released chemicals then cross the gap and bind to receptors on the target cell. There are several classes of neurotransmitters, including amino acids (such as glutamate, GABA, glycine, and aspartate), monoamines (such as dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine, and histamines), peptides (such as endorphins and oxytocin), and others (such as acetylcholine, ATP, and adenosine). Neurotransmitters can be divided into functional categories: excitatory neurotransmitters (such as glutamate, acetylcholine, dopamine, epinephrine, nitric oxide, and histamine), which initiate impulses; and inhibitory neurotransmitters (such as GABA, glycine, serotonin, and endorphin), which inhibit impulses upon binding their receptors. Bacterial toxins, such as botulinum toxin and tetanus toxin, inhibit the release of excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters, respectively, causing paralysis.
Fig.14.2. Peripheral Nerves. A. A nerve contains several sensory or motor neurons, an artery, and a vein, all covered

by a connective tissue membrane called the epineurium. The bundles of axons within are also packed by a membrane named endoneurium. B. The pathway of an impulse over a reflex arc (simplified). Note that the sensory neuron carries the sensation to the CNS. The cell body of the sensory neuron is located outside the CNS. An internuncial (i.e., connector) neuron relays the impulse to the dendrites of a motor neuron. The cell body of the motor neuron is located within the CNS. The motor neuron transmits the response to a muscle or gland through its axon. C. The electrochemical nature of neurotransmission: an impulse is transmitted through an axon as an electrical impulse generated by the opening and closing of ion channels. D. Synapse and signal transmission: as the electrical impulse reaches the end of the axon at the neural junction, it triggers the release of neurotransmitters. These neurotransmitters travel across the synaptic gap and bind to receptors on the target neuron, muscle, or gland cell. This receptor binding initiates signal transduction, leading to the next action.

blocks.text: Viral and subviral diseases

Human herpesvirus virus-1 and -2 (meningitis, encephalitis, neuralgia, latency in ganglia); Varicella Zoster virus (neuralgia and latency in ganglia); JC virus (progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy and neural damage); alphaviruses (EEEV, WEEV, VEE, SINV, and Semliki Forest virus); Crimean Congo hemorrhagic virus, Dengue virus, Human immunodeficiency virus 1 and 2, influenza virus A, Japanese encephalitis virus, Lacrosse virus, Lassa (hemorrhagic) virus, Junin virus, rabies lyssavirus, lymphochoriomeningitis virus, Machupo virus, mumps virus, Oropouche virus, poliovirus, Rift Valley fever virus, rubella virus, St. Louis encephalitis virus, various tick-borne encephalitis viruses, West Nile virus and prion agent (encephalopathy); rabies lyssavirus (hydrophobia), Borna disease virus (neurological conditions such as autism spectrum) and measles virus (subacute sclerosing panencephalopathy). Bacterial diseases Acinetobacter sp., Actinomyces sp., Borrelia burgdorferi, and related species, Burkholderia cepacia and related species, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, K. oxytoca, Leptospira interrogans and related species, Listeria monocytogenes, Neisseria meningitidis, Nocardia and related organisms, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Serratia sp., Hemophilus influenzae and related species, Streptococcus pneumoniae and many other bacteria (meningitis); Borrelia burgdorferi and related species, Chlamydophila psittaci and Treponema pallidum pallidum (encephalitis); Actinomyces sp., Nocardia asteroides and related organisms (brain abscess); Bordetella pertussis and B. parapertussis (mechanical brain damage as an aftermath of whooping cough); Clostridium botulinum (flaccid paralysis); Clostridium tetani (spastic paralysis); Campylobacter sp. (Guillain-Barre syndrome); Rickettsia prowazekii, R. typhi and Orientia tsutsugamushi (various neurological problems).
Fungal diseases

Aspergillus niger, A. fumigatus, A. flavus, A. terreus, Blastomyces dermatitidis, Coccidioides immitis, C. posadasii, Cryptococcus neoformans and Histoplasma capsulatum (meningitis, mostly among immunocompromised subjects). Parasitic diseases Protozoa: Encephalitozoon, Enterocytozoon and related species, Toxoplasma gondii, Naegleria fowleri, Balamuthia sp., and Acanthamoeba sp. (encephalopathy, brain eating disease); Plasmodium falciparum (cerebral malaria); Trypanosoma brucei (African sleeping sickness); flatworms: Paragonimus westermani (encephalopathy), Taenia solium (brain cysticercosis); Echinococcus granulosus (hydatid cysts in the brain); Toxocara canis and T. cati (encephalopathy); roundworms: Ancylostoma, Necator, and Strongyloides (meningitis due to excessive infection among immunodeficient subjects) and Trichinella spiralis (meningitis due to mass migration to the brain).

blocks.text: African sleeping sickness

This disease is caused by the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma brucei and transmitted by tsetse flies. Of the two strains of the parasite, the East African strain is more common, and it causes slow-progressing disease (about a year before symptoms arise). The West African strain causes fast-progressing disease (symptoms arise within weeks of the bite by infected flies). The initial (stage 1) signs occur while the parasite is in the blood and lymphatics, and the signs include recurrent fever, headache, and joint pain. The stage 2 signs include changes in the sleep cycle (daytime sleepiness, nighttime insomnia, and personality changes) after the parasite crosses the blood-brain barrier and enters brain tissue (Fig. 14.3). An untreated individual suffers extensive damage in the CNS, becomes comatose, and ultimately dies. Rural citizens engaged in farming and animal care are more prone to infection. Treatment options include oral fexinidazole (if detected early) and Nifurtimox-Eflornithine Combination Therapy (if detected late in the infection, with CNS involvement). The arsenic-containing, highly toxic drug (melarsoprol) is no longer used. Preventive measures include avoiding the region (i.e., sub-Saharan Africa) where the disease is endemic, staying away from bushes, and wearing white clothing (covering the whole body) impregnated with insect repellent. There is no vaccine for the disease at present.

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)

Prenatal and childhood infections by diverse pathogens, including rubella virus, cytomegalovirus, human herpes virus- 1, -2, -3, influenza A, Zika virus, SARS-CoV-2, and Borna disease virus; bacterial meningitis, Lyme disease (caused by Borrelia sp.), and parasitic infections (including Toxoplasma gondii), have been associated with ASD. However, the evidence is indirect and weak. The association of vaccines and ASD has been ruled out. ASD includes varying levels of social impairment, repetitive behaviors, learning difficulties, and heightened or atypical sensitivity to stimuli. If infections are indeed associated with ASD, infection prevention and vaccination should be ideal to reduce ASD incidence.
Brain abscess

It is a life-threatening disease that may stem from skull injury, infections in the face, mouth, teeth, and eyes, and in surgical wounds, usually among debilitated individuals with a compromised immune system. The causative agents include bacteria (especially actinobacteria), fungi, and protozoan parasites. The signs include fever, headache, confusion, lethargy, vision difficulties, stiff neck, and seizures. The lesion in the brain contains live and dead pathogens, dead cells, including dead neutrophils, and pus, surrounded by a thin wall that can be covered by a fibrous capsule over time (Fig. 14.3). The condition can be diagnosed from patient history, disease signs, and MRI or CT scan of the head, and treated with aggressive antimicrobial drugs and removal (aspiration) of the fluid from the lesion. Brain cysticercosis The disease develops among people who accidentally ingest the eggs of the pork tapeworm (Taenia solium ) in soiled food and drinks (not from consuming uncooked or undercooked pork containing the worm's larvae). Diverse organs, especially the brain (Fig. 14.4), muscles, skin (subcutaneous), and eyes, can be affected. Low-level infections of the other organs can be asymptomatic, but brain infections show many pathological signs, including seizures, headache, confusion, psychosis, and death. The disease is more common in rural areas of Africa, South America, and East Asia, where subsistence pig farming is common. About 2,000 cases of brain cysticercosis (which accounts for about 2% of cases of seizure) are reported annually in the USA, mostly among South American Immigrants. Brain cysticercosis is diagnosed by patient history and CT scan of the brain. The disease is treated with albendazole or praziquantel, along with corticosteroids (to reduce inflammation from dying cysts).

Brain-eating disease (amebic meningoencephalitis) It is a rare disease caused by the protozoan pathogen Naegleria fowleri. People contract the infection while swimming in warm freshwater lakes and rivers (the organism is considered a thermophile). Only inhalation (but not ingestion) of the parasite causes infection. The parasite travels from the nasal sinus to the brain through the olfactory nerves. The pathogen normally sustains itself by hunting bacteria. In the brain, the parasite consumes astroglial cells and neurons. Although the initial symptoms (within five days of contracting) include flu-like conditions, headache, and vomiting, the conditions soon turn to severe headache, seizure, hallucination, and death. The disease's rapid progression may prevent diagnosis and proper treatment in many cases. Definitive diagnosis requires a case history (warm water contact or nasal washing with untreated water) and PCR of DNA extracted from the brain biopsy. The disease is treated with amphotericin B, which is essentially ineffective because 97% of the patients die within 18 days of infection. Prevention of infection (avoiding swimming in warm freshwater or using such water to wash the nasal cavity) is easier. The disease is extremely rare, with fewer than 500 cases globally and fewer than 5 cases in the USA. Acanthamoeba sp., another protozoan parasite, may infect the eyes, lungs, skin, and brain. People (mostly immunocompromised individuals) in the Western Hemisphere contract amoebic keratitis through contact lenses contaminated with dirt, mud, or water (e.g., during swimming) that may contain the amoeba or through the skin to the blood. Note that Acanthamoeba sp. can survive in contact lens cleaning solutions. If the parasite enters the brain (from the eyes or blood), it triggers the formation of a granuloma in brain tissue, where it releases proteases that damage the brain. The signs of eye infection include redness and ulceration (Fig. 14.4), and those of brain infection include fever, nausea, vomiting, seizures, and death. Eye infections can be treated with anti-protozoan eye drops or corneal transplantation (if necessary); the brain infections are usually fatal. The infection can be definitively diagnosed by brain biopsy and PCR of DNA extracted from the biopsy. It is estimated that annually, around 1,500 people in the USA develop Acanthamoeba keratitis, and about 3 people contract brain infections caused by the parasite. Cerebral malaria Malaria is caused by several species of the protozoan genus Plasmodium, including P. falciparum, which may cause cerebral malaria. Female Anopheles mosquitoes transmit the parasite to humans while sucking blood. The parasite travels to the liver and infects hepatocytes. The infected hepatocytes rupture (in about 15 days) and release new instars of parasites (about 40,000/hepatocyte) that infect erythrocytes. The parasite consumes the contents of erythrocytes and replicates there for several days. The parasite then breaks the cell open, releasing the new batch of parasites and various metabolites (including hemozoin) into the blood, causing high fever and chills. The parasite infects a new batch of erythrocytes, and the cycle continues every 48-72 hours, depending on the species. If left untreated, patients suffer from massive splenomegaly and ultimately die in a few months or years after infection, of severe anemia, rupture of the spleen, and multiple organ failure (especially the lung). However, P. falciparum infections may kill the patient within 4-8 days of the initial mosquito bite. Erythrocytes infected by this species deform and become sticky. The deformed and sticky erythrocytes block the blood capillaries of the brain and cause severe symptoms, including seizures, coma, and death. The sticky cells may also affect the blood vessels of the lung and cause severe acute respiratory syndrome (ARDS), leading to death.

Malaria is detected by disease symptoms, PCR using DNA extracted from blood, or microscopic examination of erythrocytes. The disease can be treated with oral quinine (chloroquine) and artemisinin combination therapy. Malaria is one of the most prevalent infectious diseases, with about 300,000,000 new cases and over 600,000 deaths, mostly children, pregnant women, and the elderly. About 95% of malaria deaths are caused by P. falciparum. The disease is endemic in Central America, the northern part of South America, central Africa, South Asia, and the East Indies, but 90% of cases are reported from sub-Saharan Africa. The endless battle to prevent malaria through insecticide spraying had failed, though it had reduced mosquito biting to some extent. The WHO has approved two malaria vaccines that are currently available in sub-Saharan Africa for children. The vaccine is 50-70% effective in preventing malaria. CDC recommends that people traveling to areas where P. falciparum is highly prevalent take prophylactic (prescription) antimalarial drugs (such as atovaquone/proguanil, mefloquine, and doxycycline).
Encephalitis and encephalopathy

Encephalitis is a form of encephalopathy characterized by inflammation, with signs such as fever, headache, hallucinations, seizures, and stiff neck. Encephalopathy is any pathological change in normal brain function. These diseases can be caused by infection, lack of oxygen (after a stroke), accumulation of toxic metabolites due to kidney or liver failure, autoimmune reactions, etc. The signs of encephalitis include changes in the mental state, memory loss, and dementia. Note the following • Infectious encephalitis- caused by infection of the brain cells/tissues • Infection-related encephalopathy- brain function decline due to systemic infection (without brain infection) • Post-infection encephalitis- mostly due to autoimmune reactions (antibodies binding brain tissues) • Infection-triggered encephalopathy- neurological decline after high fever Section 14.1.1 gives a partial list of microbes that cause encephalitis and encephalopathy. The pathogens also affect other organs. Since encephalitis and encephalopathy are generally nonspecific signs, findings in other organs can be helpful in identifying the causative agents. Encephalopathy/encephalitis (as well as meningitis) can progress to rapid fatality (death occurs within 48-72 hours among infants and children, within 3-7 days among adults), treatments must be started as early as possible. In many cases, treatment begins even before the causative agents are detected. Survivors often live with some disabilities.

Infection-related encephalitis is relatively common in the USA, with 10-15 cases per 100,000 population and a mortality rate of 5.6% of the hospitalized cases. Children under one year or the elderly (65 and older) are the more vulnerable groups. Infection-related encephalitis is treated using a combination of (a) antimicrobial chemotherapeutic agents, (b) high doses of corticosteroids, (c) immunoglobulin therapy, and (d) supportive care (sedatives, anti-seizure medications, ventilation, pain management, and intravenous nutrients).
Rabies

A classic case of encephalitis that leads to encephalopathy is rabies. The virus enters the human body through scratches, bites, or through inhalation of aerosolized saliva from rabid animals. If the affected person receives medical care (proper wound cleaning and rabies vaccine), the patient will survive without showing any signs of rabies. For untreated victims, the virus initially infects local cells and replicates there. The progeny viruses enter the local neurons, migrate to the spinal cord, and then to the brain, where they infect the neural cell bodies. The virus replicates rapidly without killing the host cell, causing granular inclusion particles (Negri bodies) to form inside the cell (Fig. 14.4). It may take months to years after contracting the virus before initial signs of encephalitis (fever, headache, and anorexia) develop. The length of the prodrome is proportional to the distance of the inoculation site from the brain. The person develops both antibody and cell-mediated immune responses to the virus, but they are not protective (nearly all cases of symptomatic rabies are fatal). The patients subsequently develop signs of encephalopathy, such as personality changes, hydrophobia (fear of drinking water, because drinking is associated with intense pain), and ultimately die of respiratory failure and coma. Symptomatic rabies is essentially untreatable, but combined antiviral and antiserum therapy and induced coma show a possibility of saving life. A vaccine for rabies is available, but it is given to animal handlers and veterinarians. The general public gets the vaccine only if they are potentially exposed to the virus. Globally, about 10 million cases of rabies are reported annually, including 20,000 in the USA, with approximately 60,000 deaths. Coyotes, raccoons, bats, and skunks serve as reservoirs of rabies in the United States. In South America, vampire bats transmit the virus to cattle, causing the deaths of hundreds of thousands of cattle each year. In Asian countries, street and pet dogs are the primary vectors due to inconsistent animal vaccination.
Flaccid paralysis due to botulism

The endospores of Clostridium botulinum are plentiful in soil. Endospores are frequently ingested with food, but they do not germinate in the adult intestine because of competing resident gut biota. However, endospores may germinate in the intestines of infants (lacking the resident biota), in wounds, and in the anaerobic environment of improperly canned non-acidic foods. The vegetative cells secrete botulinum toxin, a type III (i.e., A-B type) toxin. The B subunit of the botulinum toxin binds receptors on nearby neurons and is taken in by endocytosis. Once inside the neuron, the A subunit leaves the endosome and is processed to become a peptidase (a protease that cleaves other proteins). The mature A subunit cleaves specific SNARE proteins involved in the release of excitatory neurotransmitters, including acetylcholine, epinephrine, glutamate, histamine, and dopamine. As a result, the affected muscles cannot contract, leading to flaccid paralysis (Fig. 14.5). The disease is also called botulism. Botulinum toxin is one of the most potent toxins known; about 1 ng/kg is lethal to an adult person. Death usually occurs more quickly if the toxin affects the lung muscles of the person.

Botulism was a major disease among sausage eaters in Europe. Since the adoption of sodium nitrite in meat processing and the implementation of industrial sterilization standards in food canning, botulism has almost disappeared from developed countries. In the United States, some 30 cases of foodborne botulism and 100 cases of infant botulism occur every year. Non-acidic canned food imported from developing countries is a potential source of foodborne botulism. Occasional outbreaks of botulism occur in Alaska, where seal flippers are fermented at low heat in wooden or metal casks. Endospores germinate in the cask, especially in metal casks, allowing botulinum to accumulate in the food. The fermented flippers are eaten without any further processing. Such food may cause acute botulism among Alaskans who eat the contaminated fermented seal flippers. C. botulinum endospores do not germinate in acidic canned food. Suspect non-acidic canned food can be heated to 85 oC to inactivate botulinum toxin. Children under 1 year old should not be given raw honey or cooked or baked foods (endospores can only be inactivated by autoclaving or pressure- cooking at 121 °C for 15 minutes). A silver lining of botulinum toxin is that it has many medical uses, including treating uncontrolled muscle movement, overactive bladder, facial wrinkles, and pain management. The US market value of medically used botulin (i.e., BotoxTM) is about $6 billion.
Fig. 14.5. Mode of action of botulinum toxin. A. A normal neuromuscular junction illustrating the steps of

neurotransmitter release. The SNARE proteins interact with the synaptobrevin proteins on vesicles loaded with excitatory neurotransmitters (such as acetylcholine). These vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane at the axon terminal and release acetylcholine, which binds to receptors on muscle cells, triggering signal transduction that leads to muscle contraction. B. A neuromuscular junction affected by botulinum toxin. The protease activity of the A subunit of the exotoxin cleaves the SNARE proteins. Consequently, the SNARE proteins cannot facilitate the fusion of vesicles loaded with acetylcholine. This failure to release acetylcholine impairs signal transduction and ultimately causes flaccid paralysis. Image is drawn after Al-Ghamadi AS, et al. J Dermatol Dermatol Surg 2015; 19(1): 1-8. Guillain-Barré syndrome This is an autoimmune disease that can occur after recovering from Zika virus, SARS-CoV-2, influenza, or Campylobacter jejuni infections. Some antibodies produced during infection by these pathogens bind to neurons and destroy them by activating complement pathways. The inflammation also triggers T cells and macrophages, leading to further inflammation. Vaccination may also cause these symptoms, but rarely. Symptoms of the disease include tingling sensations in the skin, muscle pain, temporary paralysis, and breathing difficulties. The disease is diagnosed based on clinical history and the accumulation of excess proteins in the blood and CSF. About 3,000- 10,000 people in the USA develop the disease every year. Most recover spontaneously but slowly, with a mortality less than 10%. In some cases, removal of excess antibodies through plasmapheresis, ventilation, and pain management may be necessary to treat the patients.

Hydatid cysts (see Chapter 13) Brain damage due to whooping cough (see Section 14.3.3) Meningitis Meningitis includes a group of signs and symptoms involving inflammation of the membranes of the brain. Symptoms occur when microbes (mainly viruses and bacteria, but fungi and parasites may also cause it) in the blood cross the blood-brain barrier and enter the cerebrospinal fluid. The presence of microbes and their PAMPs triggers an immune response, including leukocyte migration, release of reactive oxygen species, cytokine secretion, cytotoxic activities (cleaning infected cells), antibody deposition, and complement activation. The presence of microbes and excess leukocytes in the CSF can be assessed by fluid collected through a spinal tap. Although leukocyte migration is essential for controlling infection, it can also contribute to severe disease signs (high fever, severe headache, stiff neck, and skin rashes) in meningitis. The effects on the brain include high intracranial pressure, brain swelling (edema), and damage to brain tissue. Meningitis often appears with septicemia.

Early diagnosis and prompt medical intervention are crucial for effectively treating meningitis. Bacterial meningitis requires aggressive antibiotic treatment, while viral meningitis is generally milder and may resolve without antiviral therapy. Additional supportive care, similar to that used for encephalitis, is also important. Often, antibacterial treatments are administered before the specific causative agents are identified. Microbial analysis of CSF and PCR/RT-PCR testing using nucleic acid extracted from CSF helps identify the responsible pathogens (Fig. 14.6). Meningitis is a common disease, with approximately 2.5 million cases annually (fewer than 1,000 in the USA) and around 100,000 deaths worldwide. Bacterial meningitis, caused by pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Streptococcus agalactiae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Neisseria meningitidis, is among the deadliest, with a mortality rate of over 15%, despite the availability of effective vaccines for some of these pathogens. Newborns, infants, and the elderly are at higher risk. Many survivors of meningitis may experience mild to severe neurological impairments.

the presence of bacteria (specifically, Streptococcus sp.) and excess leukocytes. B. A Gram-stained smear of CSF of a patient showing the presence of G(-) diplococci (Neisseria meningitidis, indicated by the arrow) and many neutrophils. C. An MRI scan of a patient's head with PML showing multifocal lesions. All images are from Wikipedia. Neuralgia Neuralgia is episodic pain that follows a nerve. The pain can vary in qualities such as burning, stabbing, throbbing, and more. The root cause is nerve damage from infections (such as human herpesvirus-1, -2, and -3, Treponema pallidum, and Borrelia sp.) or noninfectious conditions (such as diabetes, kidney disease, nerve compression from tumors or other causes, and injuries). Symptoms can be triggered by unrelated stimuli like touch, movement, and temperature changes. People who have or have recovered from syphilis, Lyme disease, disseminated herpes, and shingles may show signs of the disease. Neuralgia is diagnosed through patient history and MRI. Treatment involves addressing the underlying causes, nerve blocking, medications (such as anticonvulsants), and surgery (to relieve nerve pressure).

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) PML is caused by the reactivation of the JC virus latently infecting the brain. Almost everybody is latently infected by the virus, but the virus reactivates among people with severe immunosuppression, especially among people with AIDS and subjects being treated with highly immunosuppressive drugs. The reactivated virus infects and kills glial cells, causing demyelination of axons in the brain. Lesions develop in the white matter of the brain (Fig. 14.6). The patient shows progressive signs of neurodegeneration, including weakness in the limbs, memory loss, and signs of blindness. Lack of T cell immunity allows the damage to progress to a fatal end. The disease can be detected by brain imaging and by the presence of viral DNA in the CSF (by PCR). There is no specific treatment for PML. Treatments are aimed at restoring cell-mediated immunity (by treating HIV-I and -2 infections, and reducing immunosuppression). About 30-50% of the affected subjects die within a few months of reactivation of the virus, although some people survive longer with significant disabilities.
Spastic paralysis

The disease is caused by the type III exotoxin (i.e., tetanospasmin) produced by Clostridium tetani. The bacterium cannot survive in the air, but its endospores do. Endospores may enter a soiled deep wound and germinate there. The vegetative cells emerge there and produce tetanospasmin. The toxins are released by the bacterium upon lysis. The B subunit of the A-B type toxin binds to its receptors on neurons, is taken up by endocytosis, and is transported to the neuron's cell body. The A subunit of the toxin exits the endosome and cleaves synaptobrevin, preventing the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters (such as GABA and glycine). However, the release of the excitatory neurotransmitter remains unaffected. As a result, muscles innervated by the neuron continue to contract without intermittent relaxation, leading to spastic paralysis (Fig. 14.7).
Fig. 14.7. Tetanus and SSPE. A. Uptake of the A-B tetanospasmin by the toxin receptors of a motor neuron at a

myoneural junction. B. The whole A-B toxin is transported through the axon to the cell body located in the brain or spinal cord. The A subunit of the toxin leaves the vesicle and enters the cytoplasm. C. The A subunit of the toxin destroys synaptobrevin and inhibits the release of the inhibitory neurotransmitters. Release of excitatory neurotransmitters continues, leading to chronic muscle contraction and ultimately spastic paralysis of the muscle that the motor neuron innervates. Redrawn after Bomba-Warkzac E, et al. Cell Receptors 2016; 16(7): 1974-1987. D. An infant with systemic tetanus. Note the stiffness in the neck and legs of the infant held at the feet and head. Image- Wikipedia. E. A child with SSPE, having a distorted stature. The MRI of the child’s brain (right) shows diffuse cerebral atrophy. Image- Kaur S, et al. J Move Disorders 2023;16(3):336-338. DOI: https://doi.org/10.14802/jmd.23052 It takes about 5 days for the disease to develop after exposure to tetanus endospores in a wound. Several types of clinical diseases are caused by tetanospasmin. Neonatal tetanus begins with the unhygienic removal of the umbilical stump from the newborn. Both motor neurons and sympathetic neurons can be affected in generalized tetanus. This form is characterized by a locked jaw, muscle contractions resembling a smile in the face, and severe spasms in the back muscles leading to a curved body (Fig. 14.7). The closer the injury is to the central nervous system, the faster the disease progresses and the more severe the symptoms usually are. Patients may suffer from bone fractures, muscle tears, breathing difficulties, lung and kidney failure, and ultimately death—all caused by uncontrolled muscle spasms and their aftereffects. In localized tetanus, symptoms stay confined to an affected area, such as the head (cephalic tetanus). Different receptors for tetanospasmin influence whether the disease becomes localized or generalized. Tetanus can be deadly (with a lethality rate as high as 90% in some cases). Survivors usually suffer lasting damage in the nervous system. Tetanospasmin binding to neurons is irreversible. Therefore, recovery is only possible after the neurons are regenerated.

Over a million cases of tetanus, many with fatal outcomes, occur globally each year. Contact sports on dirt and fireworks (explosions that cause small soil particles to penetrate the skin) are among the main sources of exposure to C. tetani endospores. In developed countries, a highly effective tetanus toxoid vaccine, such as the DTP vaccine, has nearly eradicated the disease. Fewer than one hundred cases are reported in the United States, mostly among the elderly who have low antibody levels to tetanospasmin. A booster shot every ten years is highly effective in preventing tetanus in older age groups.
Subacute sclerosing panencephalopathy (SSPE)

SSPE develops in children who are chronically infected with the mutant measles virus, such as defective interfering particles of the virus. Children two years old or younger with poor cell-mediated immunity, who were naturally infected by the wild-type virus, are at risk of developing the disease. The defective virus causes a persistent infection in the brain cells. Symptoms of SSPE typically appear about 6 to 10 years after the initial infection. The signs include fever, seizures, personality changes, altered body posture, memory loss, muscle spasms (Fig. 14.7), loss of movement, and death. Affected children show a poor cell-mediated immune response but an excessive antibody response, both of which contribute to the pathology of the disease. Research indicates that the live-attenuated measles vaccine does not cause SSPE.

The disease can be diagnosed through patient history, detection of viral RNA in the CSF (using RT-PCR), and imaging such as MRI or CT scans of the head. There is no cure for SSPE; patients usually die within 1 to 3 years of diagnosis. Widespread childhood vaccination has drastically reduced measles and SSPE in developed countries, but new outbreaks have been reported in many countries, including the USA. WHO estimates approximately 10 million cases of measles each year. The risk of SSPE is about 27 cases per 100,000 unvaccinated children after initial infection. The growing antivaccine sentiment, especially in Western countries like the USA, may contribute to higher incidences of measles and SSPE in the future.

blocks.text: The digestive (alimentary) system includes the mouth, oral cavity, alimentary canal, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, and associated ducts (Fig. 14.8). The mouth is divided by a line of teeth into two chambers: the vestibule at the front and the oral cavity proper at the rear. The sides of the mouth are called the cheeks. The bottom is covered by the tongue. The roof of the mouth is formed by the hard palate at the front and the soft palate at the rear. The posterior border of the soft palate is called the uvula, which hangs from the roof of the mouth. Behind the soft palate is the gullet, which connects the mouth to the tubular cavity known as the pharynx. The respiratory and digestive systems are joined at the pharynx. Lymphoid tissues, such as tonsils and adenoids, are located at the back of the mouth, at the end of the soft palate, on the roof of the pharynx, and at the base of the tongue (Fig. 14.8).

The mouth contains buccal glands throughout the oral cavity and salivary glands in three distinct locations. The salivary glands include the parotid glands, located below the ears; the submandibular glands; and the submaxillary glands, found near the lower jaw under the tongue (Fig. 14.8). The secretions of these glands (saliva) are essential for food lubrication and digestion. The tongue is composed of skeletal muscle and is crucial for properly positioning food for chewing. The tongue also contains numerous taste buds, which serve as chemosensory organs. The entire oral cavity, along with the pharynx and esophagus, is covered by a squamous epithelium.

Teeth are bony organs used for mastication (chewing). Each tooth has a visible crown and a root that fits into the bony sockets of the maxilla and mandible bones. The gum (i.e., gingiva) is soft tissue (part connective tissue, part mucosa) that loosely covers the neck of the tooth (Fig. 14.8). Under the gum, the teeth are anchored to the bony socket by ligaments (not by basement membrane or cement). The crown of the teeth is covered by enamel, the hardest tissue in the human body. Enamel consists of 97% calcified minerals (including crystalline minerals) and 3% organic molecules. The remainder of the tooth is composed of dentine, another calcified tissue (50% calcified) that encases the pulp cavity. Although stronger than dense bone, dentine is less mineralized than enamel. The pulp cavity houses blood vessels and neurons.

Structure of a tooth. Image: Linus Books.

The pharynx is a tube-like cavity divided into three sections. The nasopharynx connects directly to the nasal cavity and to the middle ear through the Eustachian canal (Fig. 14.8). The oropharynx receives food and drinks from the mouth via the gullet, passing them to the laryngopharynx and finally into the esophagus. The esophagus, approximately 25 cm long and 2 cm wide, begins at the base of the tongue and empties into the stomach. It is lined with stratified squamous epithelium interspersed with layers of connective tissue proper and smooth muscle. There is no distinct sphincter valve at either the beginning or the end of the esophagus, although the tube remains constricted to prevent a backflow of food.

The stomach is a tubular sac, shaped like a bird. It consists of three distinct regions: the fundus, the body, and the pylorus (Fig. 14.9). The stomach is covered by glandular epithelium and layers of muscle and connective tissue. Gastric glands are present in the pits of the fundus and the body of the stomach. These glands secrete mucus and gastric juice. Gastric juice contains components such as hydrochloric acid, pepsinogen (the inactive form of the protease pepsin), and vitamin B12-binding protein (intrinsic factor). At the end of the pylorus, there is a muscular sphincter (ring) that prevents the premature release of stomach contents and the backflow of intestinal contents. The entire stomach is coated with a thick layer of mucus to protect the underlying tissue from gastric acid (whose pH can be as low as 2.0) and enzymes.

The small intestine of an adult person is a 6,000 x 2 cm tube that connects the pyloric sphincter and the large intestine (Fig. 14.8). The small intestine can be divided into three parts. The duodenum is a C-shaped initial portion (about 25 cm) that receives the common ducts from the pancreas, liver, and gall bladder (Fig. 14.9). The next segment, the jejunum (about 2,500 cm), and the final segment, the ileum (about 3,500 cm), constitute the bulk of the lower abdomen (Fig. 14.9). The ileum ends with a sphincter that connects it to the large intestine. The small intestine is covered by glandular epithelium containing fingerlike projections called intestinal villi (Fig. 14.9). The villi (sing. villus) are finger-like structures at the tips of epithelial cells, increasing the absorptive surface area of the cell. The glands in the duodenum secrete juice that neutralizes stomach acid. The cells of its internal surface shed and release proteolytic enzymes that activate pre-enzymes found in the pancreatic juice (see below). Absorption occurs mainly in the jejunum, where digested food enters the cells and then into venous blood. Venous blood carries nutrients to the liver via the hepatic portal veins. The digested lipids form lipid-protein complexes (chylomicrons), which are absorbed in the intestine. However, chylomicrons are transported by lymphatic ducts. The ileum contains a large mass of lymphoid tissue called Peyer's patches (see Chapter 9).
Fig. 14.9. The stomach, intestine, and colon. A. Stomach (top) and a section through the body of the stomach

(below). B. Small intestine (duodenum) with bile and pancreatic ducts (top) and a section of a healthy intestine (below). C. Colon and appendix (top) and a section through a healthy colon (bottom). All histological slides were stained with H&E. Unlike the small intestine, the stomach and colon lack villi. The mucous membrane in each of these three areas is secretory.

The large intestine is a flat tube measuring 1,500 x 7 cm, consisting of three sections: the caecum, the colon, and the rectum (Fig. 14.10). Its primary function is to reabsorb water from the chyme (the leftover from digested food) and compact the chyme to produce and eject feces. A worm-like appendix is attached to the caecum. The appendix is not part of the digestive system; it contains lymphoid tissue. The colon is folded to form an imperfect square in the lower abdomen, encircling the small intestine. The rectum serves as a temporary repository for feces before it exits the body through the anus, which is guarded by the anal sphincter.

The liver is the largest internal organ in the body, serving over 200 functions. It has four lobes, each containing approximately 100,000 hexagonal lobules, which are separated by connective tissue. At the center of each lobule lies a vein known as the central vein (Fig. 14.10). Numerous cell plates comprising a single layer of liver cells (i.e., hepatocytes) radiate to the central vein like spokes on a wheel. The cell plates are separated by blood-filled sinusoids (a very wide capillary-like blood vessel). Blood in the sinusoids is supplied by the branches of the hepatic portal vein (see Chapter 15), which carries nutrient-rich blood from the intestine. At each of the (six or so) corners of the lobules, branches of the hepatic artery and hepatic portal veins can be found. Blood from the branches of the hepatic portal veins as well as oxygen-rich blood from the hepatic arteries flows into the sinusoids and then into the central vein. The hepatocytes absorb nutrient molecules in the blood of the hepatic portal vein to a level tolerable for the body (removing up to 25% of ingested glucose and 90% of ingested fructose, for example). Hepatocytes also secrete bile, which is necessary for digesting lipids. Bile is collected in the bile ductules (Fig. 14.10). Ductules from different lobes of the liver unite to form the common bile duct, which joins the pancreatic duct before opening into the duodenum. The pancreas is located beneath the pylorus, attached to the fold of the duodenum. This organ comprises both exocrine and endocrine components. The exocrine components consist of alkaline pancreatic juice secreted by numerous acinar cells (Fig. 14.10). This juice contains various proteases (i.e., chymotrypsinogens, trypsinogen, etc.), amylases, lipases, and nucleases, which, when activated in the intestine, digest proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids, respectively. The pancreatic juice flows into two pancreatic ducts that merge with the common bile duct and open into the duodenum. The endocrine components include glucagon and insulin (hormones) essential for regulating blood sugar levels. These hormones are secreted by alpha and beta cells, respectively, found within discrete pancreatic islets (Fig. 14.10).

the lobules, there is a branch of the hepatic portal vein, a hepatic artery, and a bile duct (shown exaggerated). The rays of hepatocytes are separated by sinusoids that converge towards the central vein. Image: ohiostate.pressbooks.pub/. B. A section of the pancreas showing acinar cells and pancreatic islets. The islet is completely covered by connective tissue. Inside the islet, there are insulin-secreting beta cells and glucagon-secreting alpha cells. Image: Linus Books. The digestive system is exposed to the environment and is constantly threatened by microbial infections from food and beverages. The oral cavity and large intestine are heavily populated by normal microbiota, including resident bacteria, fungi, and protozoa. Microbial counts in the stomach, small intestine, liver, and pancreas are relatively low. Pathogenic microbes, including viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa, and worms, may inhabit the oral cavity, stomach, intestine, colon, liver, and gall bladder and cause diverse pathologies.

sections.heading: Pathologies due to infections of the digestive system

blocks.text: Appendicitis

Inflammation of the appendix occurs due to obstruction caused by hardened fecal materials, parasites, or tumor growth. It may cause fever, nausea, abdominal pain, and swelling on the right side of the abdomen. Medical examination of the abdomen and a CT scan confirm the diagnosis. The condition demands urgent care because the inflamed appendix can rupture within 48-72 hours, leading to severe sepsis and death. The treatments include surgical (appendectomy) and supportive therapies.
Dental diseases

Dental infectious diseases include dental plaque (bacterial biofilms on teeth), dental caries (cavities in teeth), gingivitis (inflammation of the gums), periodontal diseases (gum disease involving the underlying bone), and oral herpes affecting the gums. Dental plaque is a polybacterial disease because members of several genera, including Streptococcus, Lactobacillus, Porphyromonas, Actinobacillus, Bacteroides, Treponema, and Actinomyces are involved. The availability of fermentable sugars, such as glucose and fructose, in the mouth accelerates plaque formation. Bacteria in the plaques ferment sugars, and the acids produced are exposed to dental surfaces beneath the plaques. A low pH promotes the loss of minerals (calcium phosphate) from dental enamel, particularly in areas beneath the plaque, leading to softening, discoloration, and, ultimately, the formation of cavities (Fig. 14.11). Softening and thinning of the enamel may increase sensitivity to cold, hot, or acidic foods and drinks. Dental cavities involving the pulp may cause severe pain and swelling in the gums and make affected teeth prone to fracture.

Accumulation of plaque on the surfaces of teeth adjacent to the gums triggers an inflammatory response (pain, swelling, redness, and bleeding, collectively called gingivitis) that leads to gum retraction and weakening of the tooth roots. Untreated gingivitis progresses to periodontal disease, which shows all the signs of gingivitis and additional signs such as bad breath, persistent pain, and tooth loss. Affected subjects include people with poor dental hygiene, diabetics, people with dry mouth, and individuals with a weak immune system. Gingivitis and periodontal disease allow oral bacteria to enter the blood, which may lead to more serious conditions such as bacteremia, endocarditis, and actinomycosis (pus-filled granulomas in the jaw, caused by Actinomyces israelii). Reducing intake of sugary foods, washing the mouth after eating sweet substances, regular flossing, and toothbrushing with fluoridated toothpaste (to harden dental enamel) of an alkaline pH may help prevent dental plaque and caries. Good dental hygiene practices should be instituted among children. Regular dental check-ups allow early detection of weakened enamel, cavities, and recessed gums. Efforts to develop vaccines to prevent dental caries have not yet materialized. Note that people with poor mucosal immunity suffer from severe forms of dental disease despite good dental hygiene. Thus, good health and a functional immune system are always a necessity.

Gastroenteritis, diarrhea, cholera, dysentery, and other related diseases Gastroenteritis is inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract due to infection. Diarrhea is passing watery or loose stools more than three times in 24 hours, generally accompanied by an urgency (or loss of control), cramps, nausea, and vomiting. Diarrhea can be caused by infections of diverse microbes, noninfectious causes such as drug effects, and autoimmune diseases, such as irritable bowel disease (IBD). Diarrhea can be acute or chronic, and with or without blood loss. Diarrhea causes dehydration, blood loss in case of bloody diarrhea, loss of electrolytes (Na+, Cl-, K+, Mg+, HCO3-), and blood thickening, leading to diverse pathologies, including stomach cramps, malabsorption (lack of absorption of nutrients from ingested food), nausea, hypotension, organ failure, coma, and death. Viral diarrhea is usually acute (sudden onset), watery, and non-bloody, caused mainly by impaired water reabsorption by virus-infected intestinal epithelial cells. The affected subject may also have fever and other virus-specific signs. Children are more prone to viral diarrhea. The disease is usually treated with oral or intravenous saline solution (to replenish water and electrolytes). Oral saline can be homemade by mixing 1 teaspoon of table salt and 12 teaspoons of sugar into 2 liters of water. Injectable saline contains 0.9 % NaCl, about 5% glucose, and 0.15-0.3% KCl in pyrogen- free distilled water. Note that ordinary distilled water can have bacterial endotoxins (pyrogens). Bacterial diarrhea includes ordinary diarrhea with or without blood in the stool (caused by Salmonella enterica, Campylobacter jejuni, Clostridium perfringens, Vibrio vulnificus, V. parahaemolyticus, Staphylococcus aureus, Yersinia pestis, E. coli, etc.), cholera (Vibrio cholerae and certain strains of E. coli), dysentery (Shigella spp.), and colitis (Bacillus anthracis and Clostridium difficile). Many cases of bacterial diarrhea are associated with bacterial exotoxins. Cholera toxins and anthrax toxins act by activating adenylate cyclase. The excess cAMP triggers signals that cause water and electrolyte loss. Cholera is characterized by rapid dehydration and passage of milky stool. Patients may die within 2-12 hours if water and electrolytes are not replenished. Diarrhea caused by B. anthracis (always occurs after consuming meat contaminated with exotoxins of the bacterium) is caused by edema toxin and lethal toxin that kill cells (tissue damage) and increase cAMP levels. Thus, the diarrhea is bloody. Diarrhea caused by C. difficile occurs only among people being treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics. The endospores of the bacterium germinate in the intestine only if the normal biota of the intestine is severely depleted. The disease is caused by exotoxins released by C. difficile, which inflict severe injury to intestinal tissues. The disease, known as pseudomembranous colitis (Fig. 14.11), is chronic, and the affected patient may die because of malabsorption and severe intestinal damage. Bacterial (bacillary) dysentery involves diarrhea, with significant amounts of blood and mucus in the stool. The disease is caused by the Shiga toxin released by the bacterium and by the immune response triggered by its presence in the intestinal mucosa. Bacterial diarrhea requires immediate electrolyte replacement (and hydration) and, in most cases, antibiotic therapy. For diarrhea and colitis caused by C. difficile, antibiotics are ineffective; instead, the antibiotic is temporarily discontinued, and fecal transplant (enema of diluted feces from a first-degree blood relative or oral encapsulated stool) is used for therapy. Diarrhea caused by protozoa (members of the genera Balantidium, Giardia, Entamoeba, Cyclospora, Isospora and Cryptosporidium) is mostly due to immune responses (inflammatory responses), although some (Entamoeba and Cryptosporidium) release proteases in the intestinal mucosa they infect. The disease is treated by hydration and antiprotozoal medications (such as metronidazole and nitazoxanide) if necessary.
Diphtheria

Diphtheria is caused by the bacterium Corynebacterium diphtheriae (and a few related species), which is lysogenized by a bacteriophage (i.e., corynephage) that expresses diphtheria toxin (DT). DT is a type III (A-B type) exotoxin encoded by the bacteriophage's genome. C. diphtheriae not infected by corynephages are found in the throat of healthy people and do not cause diphtheria. The B subunit of DT helps the A subunit enter the host cell; the A subunit inactivates a translation elongation factor (EF2) and inhibits protein synthesis, killing the affected cell. Naïve (i.e., unvaccinated) children exposed to the disease-causing strains of C. diphtheriae usually develop symptoms within 7 days. The bacterium grows in the throat, causing fever, severe sore throat with exudative (fluid-releasing) pharyngitis, and in some children, a swollen neck (Fig. 14.12). The exudate, dead and live host cells, bacteria, fibrin clots, and other debris accumulate on the throat and tongue, forming a thick crust called the diphtheria membrane. This membrane can be pulled with forceps (Fig. 14.12). The membrane adheres tightly to the tissue underneath, so it cannot be peeled away without bleeding. In severe infections, diphtheria toxin may enter the bloodstream and affect cells in distant organs. Because neurons and heart muscle cells have many receptors for the toxin, these tissues are most affected. Respiratory blockage and cardiac arrhythmia may develop, leading to coma and ultimately death. Fig. 14. 12. Diseases caused by C. diphtheriae. A. Gram-stained bacteria (size- 0.3-0.8 x 1.0-8.0 μm). Note the ball- and-rope and horseshoe-like appearance of some of the bacteria. Image courtesy: Dr. PB Smith/CDC. B. A ten-year- old child with severe diphtheria developed a swollen neck (the bull neck). Image courtesy: CDC/Barbara Rice. C. Diphtheria membrane on the palate of a child. Image- Wikipedia. D. Ulcerative diphtheria. Shown is a photograph of an ulcerative diphtheria wound without a diphtheria membrane in the leg of a patient. Image courtesy: CDC. Disease-causing strains of C. diphtheriae can also cause skin ulcers that heal slowly (Fig. 14.12), which can be secondarily infected with Staphylococcus aureus. If enough exotoxin is produced at the ulcer site, systemic symptoms of diphtheria may develop. Patients who recover may not develop immunity to the bacterium or the toxin. Diphtheria is diagnosed by the diphtheria membrane (diagnosis of the bacterium is unnecessary) and treated by antiserum (to inactivate DT) and antibiotics (to kill the bacterium). Routine childhood DTap vaccination has almost eradicated the disease in developed countries. Fewer than 25,000 cases are reported each year globally, mostly in South and East Africa.

Gastritis and gastric cancer caused by Helicobacter pylori About 90% of patients with stomach cancer are also infected with H. pylori. The bacterium releases urease, an enzyme that breaks down urea found in body fluids into ammonia and CO2. Ammonia is a weak base that creates a buffer zone around the bacterium, allowing it to survive the extremely low pH (about 2.0) of the stomach. It also removes the thick mucus layer that protects the stomach wall from stomach acid. Contact with acid causes an inflammatory response in the stomach, initiating gastritis (inflammation of the stomach). The presence of the bacterium in the stomach and the stomach injuries chronically activate the immune system. The bacterium also secretes toxins that kill cells in the stomach lining and contribute to metaplasia (a radical but reversible change in the phenotype of cells in a tissue) and dysplasia (irreversible transformation of cells). Leucocytes migrate to inflamed areas and release ROS and NO to kill bacteria, but they also cause DNA damage in the epithelial cells of the stomach and the lymphocytes in the MALT of the stomach. If left untreated, some of these cells may develop into tumors and later into cancer cells. Most of the stomach cancers are adenocarcinomas (Fig. 14.13).

CD44 protein. B. Metaplasia in the mucosa after H. pylori infection, identified by expression of CD44 (cell stained intensely red). C. Dysplasia in the mucosa showing cells extensively expressing CD44 and changes in the structure of the tissue. CD44 is a cell surface molecule involved in cell attachment. Image- Giraud J, et al. 2017; DOI:10.5772/intechopen.69947.

Initial H. pylori infection causes abdominal pain, bloating, nausea, and loss of appetite (feeling full before satiety). Stomach cancer shows the same signs in a more severe form (abdominal pain with a burning sensation) and additional signs such as difficulty swallowing, black stool, anemia, and weight loss. H. pylori can be detected by PCR, by antibody tests, and by the production of CO2 from urea. Stomach cancer can be detected by endoscopy and CT scans. The bacterial infection can be treated with antibiotics (amoxicillin, clarithromycin, etc.) and acid inhibitors (e.g., omeprazole). Eradication of bacteria usually alleviates many symptoms, and cancer may go into remission. Additional therapy may be necessary in some cases of stomach cancer. Eradication of H. pylori does not provide immunity against future reinfection. H. pylori infection is a zoonosis (it normally infects cats and dogs), but it can also be transmitted person to person through saliva. The risk of reinfection is relatively high. Approximately 35% of the US population is infected with H. pylori, and about 1-3% of those infected develop stomach cancer.

Hepatitis, hepatomegaly, jaundice, liver fibrosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma Hepatitis is inflammation of the liver, particularly hepatocytes. It can be caused by infections (of various hepatitis viruses and other viruses), alcohol abuse, and autoimmunity. The disease results from the death of hepatocytes, thereby reducing the liver's ability to produce many of the proteins it normally produces and to process bilirubin (a pigment produced by the breakdown of erythrocytes). The signs of the acute disease include fatigue, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, dark urine, and pale stool. Since about 250 billion erythrocytes naturally die every day, the amount of bilirubin produced in the body is substantial (about 0.3 grams). Jaundice occurs due to reduced excretion (and bodily accumulation) of bilirubin, resulting in yellowing of the skin and eyes (Fig. 14.14).

About 20-90% of cases of hepatitis due to the hepatitis B virus and 1-5% of cases of hepatitis C virus infection, as well as all cases of sustained alcohol abuse, culminate in chronic hepatitis, which involves continuous death and regrowth of hepatocytes (liver repair) and activation of the liver stellate cells. Over time, the liver gets larger (develops hepatomegaly). Some of these activated stellate cells differentiate into myofibroblasts. The myofibroblasts secrete excess collagen fibers, leading to liver fibrosis (and later, cirrhosis). The collagen matrix subsequently interconnects and alters the liver's internal structure, leading to compression of the blood vessels and increased hepatic blood pressure. Chronic inflammation exposes liver cells (hepatocytes) to excess ROSs and reactive nitrogen compounds, which may cause mutations. Some of these mutated cells may become tumors and ultimately liver cancer (hepatocellular carcinoma, Fig. 14.14).

conjunctiva. Image- Wikipedia. B. A CT scan of the liver showing hepatocellular carcinoma (indicated by the arrow). Image- Hsiao C-H, et al. IEEE J Biomed Health Info. 2024; DOI:10.1109/JBHI.2024.3400599. C. Biliary obstruction by liver flukes. Shown is a rabbit bile duct infected by the fluke Chlonorchis sinensis. Note the extensive hyperplasia of the mucosa (indicated by the arrows); the bile duct is completely obstructed by the fluke. Image: Lim JH. Korean J Radiol. 2011; 12(3): 269-79. DOI:10.3348/kjr.2011.12.3.269.

Hepatitis can be diagnosed using clinical signs, biochemical tests (i.e., liver panel), detection of viruses (by PCR or RT-PCR using nucleic acid extracted from blood), ultrasound, MRI, and liver biopsy. Hepatitis caused by HAV, HEV, and other viruses (such as adenovirus and yellow fever viruses) usually resolves without any specific treatment (supportive treatment enhances recovery). There is no treatment at this point for hepatitis caused by HBV (alone or with HDV), although antiviral drugs (such as entecavir) and interferon therapy may prevent fibrosis and liver cancer. Chronic hepatitis caused by HCV is now treatable using antiviral drugs, such as combination antivirals (such as Zepatier), or ribavirin, and interferon-alpha. Fibrosis cannot be treated, although treating the underlying infections may prolong life. Liver cancer can be treated with liver resection, local chemo- or radiotherapy, or liver transplantation.

About 250 million people around the globe have HBV infection, and 50 million have HCV infection (including 1-2 million US citizens with HBV, and 2-5 million with HCV). More than 60% of the infected people are unaware of their infections and do not seek treatment. About 25% of the chronically HBV-infected subjects and about 1-4% of chronically HCV-infected subjects develop hepatocellular carcinoma. The total global economic burden due to HBV and HCV infection is close to a trillion dollars. There is a vaccine for HBV (up to 95% effective), but no vaccine for HCV. Both HBV and HCV can be transmitted sexually and vertically from mother to child, and laterally through contact with contaminated blood. Since the diseases are treatable, screening and early treatment can be beneficial in countries with very high incidence rates. Health care workers should assume that every patient is infected with HBV, HCV, HIV, and tuberculosis and handle the patients and pathological samples with due caution.

Hydatid cysts (see Chapter 13) Parotitis and inflammation of other salivary glands Salivary glands can be infected by viruses (e.g., mumps virus, influenza virus, or HIV) or bacteria (such as Staphylococcus aureus). The parotid glands are most often infected, leading to parotitis (Fig. 14.15), with signs including painful swelling of the glands, reduced saliva flow, and pain during eating and swallowing. Viral parotitis is usually bilateral, while bacterial infections are one-sided. Viral parotitis (most caused by the mumps virus) lacks specific therapy; rest and supportive care usually suffice. Bacterial parotitis is treated with antibiotics. Because of the effective mumps vaccine, parotitis is rare in the United States, with about 5,000 cases per year.

Intestinal anthrax (see diarrhea) Liver abscess, liver rot, bile duct obstruction An abscess is a pus-filled cavity with a wall, formed by infection and inflammation (see brain abscess). Liver abscess is commonly caused by bacteria (such as E. coli, Fusobacterium sp., and Klebsiella sp.), and protozoa (Entamoeba histolytica). Diabetes, preexisting biliary duct disease, and a poor immune system are risk factors. Signs include fever, right upper abdominal pain, jaundice, and a change in stool color. The disease can be detected by a CT scan and treated by drainage and antimicrobial therapy.

Liver rot is liver damage caused by liver fluke infection, as the worms bore and migrate through liver tissue until they reach and settle in the gallbladder. Early disease signs include severe belly pain, nausea, and hepatomegaly. After the parasite takes over and obstructs the bile duct, the patient may develop jaundice. Some patients develop bile duct cancer. The disease can be treated with praziquantel.
Perihepatitis

Perihepatitis is the inflammation of the peritoneum covering the liver, caused by sexually transmitted infections caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis. The disease is characterized by sharp pain in the right upper abdomen. It is associated with pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), which occurs only in sexually active women. The bacteria enter the body cavity by attaching to the spermatozoa. Some spermatozoa carry bacteria through the uterus, into the fallopian tube, and ultimately into the abdominal cavity, where the bacteria infect the peritoneum. Other signs of PID include fever, nausea, vaginal discharge, and blockage of the fallopian tubes, which can lead to ectopic pregnancy (the fetus starts growing in the fallopian tube, instead of the uterus) and female sterility (see Chapter 15). Perihepatitis may affect about one-third of women with PID. PID is quite common in the USA, with over 1 million cases each year. The disease can be treated with antibiotics.
Pigbel

Pigbel (pork-belly) is caused by Clostridium perfringens, which secretes beta-toxin (an exotoxin) that kills intestinal cells and causes necrotic conditions (Fig. 14.15). The source of the bacterium (endospores) is undercooked pork. Even well-cooked contaminated pork can transmit the bacterium through its heat-stable endospores. Affected individuals are either severely maltreated, producing very little trypsin (to destroy the beta toxin), or people who eat sweet potato, which contains trypsin inhibitors. The disease is more common in New Guinea, where sweet potato and pork are staples. Symptoms include abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, intestinal obstruction, and death. The disease can be detected by the presence of C. perfringens in stool, PCR of DNA extracted from feces, and imaging techniques such as X-ray or CT scan, and treated with antibiotics. Surgery may be necessary if the intestinal damage is substantial. Addressing underlying nutritional conditions is essential for full recovery.

Pseudomembrane colitis (see diarrhea) Proctitis and pruritus ani (due to pinworm infection) Female pinworms (Enterobius vermicularis) migrate to the rectum, move out through the anus to lay eggs in the perianal region. The worm may enter the vagina after laying eggs. The migration causes severe irritation and inflammation. The movement occurs mostly at night, which causes sleep deprivation. Children are more often infected, and they may use their fingers to relieve itching, causing rectal injuries. The disease can be diagnosed by rectal inflammation and microscopic examination of perianal samples. Perianal samples are collected with adhesive tape and examined microscopically to detect worm eggs. The disease can be treated with mebendazole or albendazole, given two doses one week apart to prevent reinfection. Children playing with sand and soil may get reinfected even after a two-dose treatment. Pinworm infection is extremely common, with a global estimate of 1 billion cases, including 30 million cases in the USA. E. vermicularis does not infect mammals other than humans. Since albendazole is highly effective in killing pinworms, pinworm infection can be effectively eradicated.
Reye’s syndrome

Children under 12 infected with influenza or human herpesvirus-3 and treated with aspirin may develop this rare disease. Early signs include persistent vomiting and lethargy, which may progress to brain edema, seizure, convulsion, and coma. The disease causes severe liver injury, indicated by elevated liver enzymes in the blood. The disease can be diagnosed using blood levels of liver-specific enzymes, a liver biopsy, and a brain scan. There is no specific treatment for the disease, although supportive therapies (intravenous glucose, mannitol, and ventilation) may help spontaneous recovery. Since viral infections are difficult to distinguish, childhood fever should be managed with acetaminophen (for children under 6) and ibuprofen (for children over 6). The disease is extremely rare in the United States at present, most likely due to the complete stoppage of aspirin in treating children.
Thrush

Thrush is an opportunistic infection caused by several Candida species (mostly by C. albicans). Although thrush can affect the skin, most cases occur in the mouth, vagina, and intestine, where the sores appear as creamy white patches (a pseudomembrane) termed cottage cheese lesions (Fig. 14.15). The rashes are itchy and painful. Thrush is more common among infants, the elderly, and people with severely low cell-mediated immunity (including patients with AIDS and cancer). The disease may progress to blood (disseminated) infection in severely immunodeficient subjects. Thrush can be treated with antifungal agents such as nystatin and echinocandins, but underlying immune dysfunction should be addressed. About 4 million cases, including over 20,000 invasive thrush cases, are reported in the USA annually.
Vitamin B12 deficiency due to infection

Dietary vitamin B12 is released from food in the stomach (due to the low pH) and is absorbed in the distal ileum. H. pylori degrades cells that synthesize intrinsic factor, a protein that binds vitamin B12 and helps its absorption. Besides H. pylori infection, excessive bacterial growth in the ileum and infection with the fish tapeworm (Diplobothrium latum) may cause vitamin B12 deficiency because the microbes consume vitamin B12. Vitamin B12 is necessary for diverse physiological functions, including erythrocyte production and DNA synthesis. Vitamin B12 deficiency is characterized by anemia, fatigue, neurological issues (including tingling sensation and memory loss), and mouth sores. Treating the infections and taking vitamin supplements can resolve these issues.
