blocks.text: The respiratory system consists of the nose, nasal cavity, paranasal sinuses, nasopharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchial tree, and lungs (Fig. 14.16). Its main function is gas exchange. The nostrils, the external openings of the nose, have coarse hairs that filter dust and other particles. Three folded structures called nasal conchae hang from the lateral walls of the nasal cavity, creating narrow spiral passages. The total area of the internal surfaces of an adult person’s nose is about 160 sq cm (25 sq inches). These narrow spaces help direct airflow through moist, blood-rich epithelia, which filter out more particles and moisten the air to nearly 100% humidity. The cool air is also warmed to near body temperature before it enters the pharynx and lungs (however, the nose cannot cool hot air to near body temperature). Paranasal sinuses are located within the bony chambers. These cavities are lined with a mucous membrane and have a narrow opening to the nasal cavities (Fig. 14.16). The sinuses produce mucus and help reduce the weight of the head. The nasal cavity connects to the eyes via the nasolacrimal ducts. The back of the nasal cavity links into the nasopharynx through the internal nares. The Eustachian tube, which emerges from the middle ear, also opens into the nasopharynx. The entire nasal cavity, including the paranasal sinuses and the nasopharynx, is covered with columnar epithelium.
Fig. 14.16. The respiratory system. A. The system is depicted, with the upper (U) and lower (L) respiratory organs
marked. B. The nose and nasopharynx are enlarged to illustrate the sinuses, nasal conchae, nasolacrimal ducts, tonsils, Eustachian canal, and epiglottis. Image: Linus Books.

The larynx (i.e., voice box) is located right at the base of the tongue and is the uppermost portion of the trachea (Fig. 14.17). Several cartilages, ligaments, and the hyoid bone form the supporting structure of the larynx. The opening of the larynx is the glottis. The glottis is partly covered by ligaments known as the ventricular and vocal folds (also called vocal cords). Inhaled air forced through the glottis produces sound as it resonates within the vocal folds. The sound is converted to voice after being articulated by the tongue, teeth, nose, palate, and paranasal sinuses. The epiglottis, a muscular flap supported by the hyoid bone, completely covers the glottis during swallowing, preventing food from entering the trachea.

The trachea, or windpipe, is an 11x2.5 cm flexible tube made of a series of C-shaped cartilages alternated with annular ligaments. The trachea is connected to the esophagus. The internal surface of the trachea is covered with a partially stratified columnar epithelium. The tube bifurcates at the end to form the primary bronchi, which enter the left and right lungs. Within the lungs, the primary bronchi divide into several secondary bronchi, which in turn divide into many tertiary bronchi (Fig. 14.17). These bronchial structures are supported by cartilage. The tertiary bronchi further divide into numerous bronchioles. Bronchioles lack cartilage support but are surrounded by smooth muscle. The bronchioles then divide into terminal bronchioles, which supply air to the pulmonary lobules. Within the pulmonary lobule, the terminal bronchiole divides into respiratory bronchioles and, eventually, into bronchial ducts. Bronchial ducts supply air to individual alveolar sacs. Each alveolar sac consists of several alveoli (sing. alveolus). The total surface area of about 400,000,000 alveoli of an adult lung is about 100 sq meters (about a tennis court). The extensively branched bronchial tree and the alveoli, along with the extensive blood and lymph vessels, are contained within the lobes of the lungs.

The alveoli are composed of simple squamous epithelium supported by connective tissue (elastic fibers). There are surfactant cells in the alveolar lining that secrete a soapy fluid that reduces surface tension and prevents the alveoli from collapsing. A few macrophages are present in the alveoli to guard the sac from microbial infections. Air in the alveoli never comes into direct contact with body fluids. Blood capillaries are located on the outer surface of the alveoli. Oxygen diffuses through the surfactant fluid, the alveolar epithelium, the basement membrane, the endothelial cells (about 1.5 μm of solid obstacle), and blood plasma to reach a red blood corpuscle (Fig. 14.17). Carbon dioxide (in plasma and red blood cells) diffuses out of the blood and enters the alveoli by crossing the same obstacles. Since CO2 and O2 are permeable to lipid membranes, diffusion occurs readily. Air enters the lungs due to the movement of the chest and diaphragm. The diaphragm is a thick muscular flap that separates the chest from the abdomen. When relaxed, the chest is slightly smaller, and the diaphragm maintains a curved shape. Upon muscle contraction, the chest expands, and the diaphragm flattens. The resulting increase in lung volume causes inhalation. The exhalation (expiration) is automatic and results from muscle relaxation.
Fig. 14.17. Larynx, bronchi, and alveoli. A. The larynx (bottom) and the components of the vocal fold (top) are

displayed. B. The bronchial tree begins at the bronchus and concludes at the terminal bronchiole (see text for details). C. A cluster of alveoli along with its blood supply and the direction of blood flow are illustrated (venules- blue, arterioles- red). D. Gaseous exchange in the alveoli is represented schematically. Gas exchange involves the diffusion of gases across blood vessels and the walls of the alveoli. Images: Linus Books.

An average adult inhales about 500 ml of air with each breath (~11,500 liters a day). Depending on air quality, a person may intake many microbes, including bacteria, fungi, bacterial and fungal spores, viruses, and worm eggs. The upper respiratory tract is inhabited by resident microbiota (bacteria and fungi), while the lower respiratory system should be sterile. Some resident microbes, as well as many pathogenic ones, including viruses and bacteria, may infect the nasal cavities, pharynx, and lymphoid tissues of the pharynx, epiglottis, larynx, bronchi, or lungs. Inflammation in the lungs (due to microbial infection) can cause fluid accumulation in the bronchi and alveoli. This fluid accumulation may obstruct oxygenation of the blood, leading to respiratory failure.

The respiratory system is divided into the upper (nose, nasal cavity, sinuses, mouth, pharynx, and larynx) and lower (trachea and the rest of the organs below) respiratory systems. Infection and inflammation of various components of the system are rhinitis (for the mucous membrane of the nose), sinusitis (for the sinuses), stomatitis (of the mouth), pharyngitis (for the pharynx), laryngitis (for the larynx), tracheitis (for the trachea), bronchitis (for the bronchi), bronchiolitis (for the bronchioles), alveolitis, pneumonitis and pneumonia (for the alveoli). Pneumonia and pneumonitis are different because the former is due to a microbial infection and involves fluid accumulation in the lungs, whereas the latter involves inflammation due to noninfectious causes (such as allergies, radiation, or chemotherapy) and usually does not involve fluid accumulation. An affected person usually suffers from multiple of these ailments simultaneously.
The Eye

The eyes are intimately connected with the brain and nose (Fig. 14.18). An adult's eye is a ball, about 2.4 cm in diameter, located in the orbital socket of the cranium. The ball consists of three concentric layers of tissue. The outermost layer comprises two components: the sclera, a thick, opaque white connective tissue in the posterior region, and the cornea, a transparent connective tissue in the anterior region. The cornea is covered by the conjunctiva, a thin mucous membrane. The second tissue layer consists of three components: the choroid, a pigmented membrane at the rear, and the ciliary body (smooth muscle) and iris at the front. The ciliary body is attached to a biconvex lens through ligaments and divides the eye into two chambers. The anterior chamber is filled with watery aqueous humor, while the posterior chamber contains jelly-like vitreous humor. The third tissue layer, the retina, only covers the posterior chamber. The retina is a sensory epithelium comprising several million light-sensitive cells known as rods and cones. Rods and cones are connected to sensory neurons, which converge to form the optic nerve that exits the eye at the back of the orbit.
Fig. 14.18. The eye and ear are closely related to the nose and mouth. A. Schematic presentation of a section of

an eye. The eye is connected to the nasal cavity through the lacrimal duct (bottom). The lacrimal duct is at the bottom of the lacrimal sac (not shown). The locations of the lacrimal gland and meibomian glands are indicated. B. Structure of the ear. The middle ear is connected to the oral cavity through the Eustachian canal. Ligaments connecting the ear ossicles (bones) to the cranium are not shown. Images: Linus Books.

The optic nerve is covered by the dura mater, one of the brain’s meninges. Through the center of the optic nerve, the retinal artery and vein enter the eyeball and perfuse the choroid. The lens and retina receive no blood supply. The eyeball is moved by six different skeletal muscles attached to it. The conjunctiva is partly covered by the eyelids that are margined with special hairs called eyebrows. The conjunctiva and eyelid surfaces are coated by a thin film of tears secreted by the lacrimal gland, an almond-shaped gland located beneath the upper edge of the orbit, behind the eyebrow. Excess tears are drained away by two lacrimal ducts. These ducts converge to form the nasolacrimal duct, which empties into the nasal cavity. Many meibomian glands (Fig. 14.18) on the eyebrow line secrete oily substances to prevent drying of the eye.

The conjunctiva and eyelids contain resident microbiota, predominantly skin bacteria. The eyes can be infected by viruses, bacteria, and, less frequently, by fungi, protozoa, and worms. Viral and bacterial eye infections, along with the resulting inflammation of the conjunctiva (conjunctivitis or pink eye), are among the primary eye ailments. Bacteria may infect the hair follicles of the eyebrows, causing a stye. Protozoa from dirt, dirty water, or contaminated contact lenses may cause conjunctival ulcers. Demodex mites (Demodex folliculorum), normally found in the hair follicles of the face, may occupy follicles of the eyelashes and cause inflammation. Blood-borne worm eggs or larvae can lodge in the eye muscles or the eyeball, causing mechanical issues. The eye is also a significant site of allergic inflammation.
The ear

The ear is a sensory organ for hearing and balance. The ears are anatomically connected to the brain and mouth. The ear is divided into three regions: the external ear, the middle ear, and the inner ear (Fig. 14.18). The external ear consists of the pinna (a skin-covered, curved cartilage that collects sound waves), a shallow ear canal (2.5 cm x 0.7 cm), and an eardrum made of a thin tympanic membrane. The skin of the ear canal contains ceruminous glands that secrete earwax. The middle ear is a small air-filled chamber connected to the oral cavity through the Eustachian canal (3.5 cm). The Eustachian canal is normally closed but can be opened by lowering the jaw. Opening the Eustachian canal is necessary to equalize air pressure differences between the ear canal and the middle ear. The eardrum connects to the inner ear via three small bones (malleus, incus, and stapes, collectively called the ear ossicles), allowing sound waves to be efficiently transmitted to the inner ear. The inner ear is deeply embedded in the cranial bones, where the cochlea (the organ of hearing) and the semicircular canals and vestibule (organs for the senses of gravity and motion) are located.

The outer and middle ears contain normal microbiota comparable to those of the skin and mouth. The inner ear is normally sterile. The external ear can be infected by soil and water bacteria (mostly Pseudomonas aeruginosa) and skin bacteria (mostly staphylococci and streptococci). Earwax has antimicrobial activity, but molds may grow in it. Ear canal infections and inflammation (otitis externa) are generally called swimmer’s ear, but can be malignant (i.e., necrotizing, involving bone damage). The middle ear can become infected with external bacteria if the eardrum ruptures. However, most middle ear infections and inflammation (otitis media) are caused by oral bacteria that enter the middle ear through the Eustachian tube. Although viruses usually do not infect the middle ear, they may contribute to middle ear maladies by infecting the tonsils and other oral surfaces, potentially blocking the Eustachian tube. Blockage of the Eustachian canal creates anaerobic conditions in the middle ear. Bacterial infections of the middle ear may also cause inflammation and blockage of the Eustachian tube. Such a blockage may increase pressure in the middle ear (due to gases released by bacteria infecting the middle ear), which can result in eardrum rupture. Inner ear infections and inflammation (labyrinthitis) are rare but may arise from middle ear infections (mostly bacterial) or through meningitis (viral, bacterial, or rarely fungal). A major sign of labyrinthitis is partial loss of hearing and balance (vertigo). Vertigo is characterized by dizziness and a sensation of the body spinning, even when the affected person is stationary. Labyrinthitis caused by middle ear infection is limited to one ear, whereas meningitis may affect both ears.

blocks.text: African river blindness

It is an endemic disease, caused by the nematode worm Onchocerca volvulus (transmitted by blackflies) in sub- Saharan Africa, where about 18 million people are currently infected. The disease signs include itchy skin nodules, eye nodules, and blindness (Fig. 14.19), about 1-2 years after initial transmission. The disease can be detected by a skin biopsy and treated with ivermectin. WHO is working to eradicate the disease through mass medication and control of blackfly populations. Several countries have reported zero new cases in recent years.
Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)

ARDS is an acute form of pneumonia, involving rapid fluid accumulation in the alveoli, leading to severe shortness of breath, rapid breathing, cough, cyanosis (bluish skin, indicating lack of blood oxygen), confusion, and death. The disease can be triggered by sepsis, viruses, including SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 infection, as well as noninfectious causes such as trauma, drowning, and smoke inhalation. Treatment mainly involves supportive therapy, such as oxygenation. Antimicrobial agents are administered for infection-related ARDS. The mortality rate for ARDS is about 30-50%. ARDS is common in the United States, with an estimated 170,000 cases, accounting for about 3.5% of all Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admissions. Globally, ARDS accounts for 10% of all ICU admissions. Bronchitis and bronchiolitis Bronchitis is inflammation of the airways (larger than bronchioles), featuring cough, wheezing, fever, fatigue, and chest pain. Most bronchitis cases are caused by cold and flu viruses, but bacterial infection may also cause the symptoms. The disease is not treated (especially for viral diseases), and most patients recover completely. However, the symptoms may persist for longer and develop into chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) if they last more than 3 months and if they involve alveolar damage (emphysema). COPD, as the name implies, is due to restricted airflow into the lungs, and its symptoms include chest tightness, shortness of breath, and a productive cough. Smokers are more vulnerable to bronchitis and COPD. COPD and chronic bronchitis with emphysema are treated with behavioral changes, supportive therapies, and ventilation when necessary. About 5% of the US population develops bronchitis and COPD each year, with costs totaling about $30 billion. Over 0.2 billion people globally suffer from COPD.

Bronchiolitis is inflammation of the bronchioles, the tubes that connect the airway with the alveoli. The disease is caused primarily by viruses, and children under 6 months of age are the most affected group. The disease is diagnosed by physical examination and usually treated by supportive therapy.

Common cold The common cold is an inflammation of the upper respiratory tract, including the nose, sinuses, throat, and pharynx, most often caused by rhinoviruses and some other viruses. Eyes may also be affected. Symptoms include a runny nose, congestion, and watery or pink eyes. Low-grade fever, body aches, and dehydration may also occur. Viruses kill epithelial cells, which release bradykinin and histamine, which bind their receptors, triggering inflammation. Excessive use of facial tissues can cause skin and nasal damage, leading to injuries and secondary bacterial infections. The common cold is the most widespread infectious disease in the United States, with about a billion cases annually— each person experiences 3-4 colds per year. Although most cases resolve spontaneously within 7-20 days, they result in many doctor visits and lost work hours, costing approximately $1.5 billion dollars in economic losses. Diagnosis is based on clinical signs, and treatment is supportive. Vitamin C intake and facial tissues infused with vitamin C may help speed recovery. Frequent, proper handwashing and wearing an N95 mask during flu season can be protective. The cold induces a cell-mediated mucosal immune response that appears to protect against more virulent pathogens. Conjunctivitis, corneal ulcer, keratitis, and trachoma Conjunctivitis is the inflammation of the conjunctiva (the membrane over the cornea) of the eye caused by bacterial (mostly Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and Chlamydia trachomatis) or viral (adenovirus, rhinovirus, and many other viruses) infections, or due to type I hypersensitivity to pollen or microbial antigens. Keratitis is a more severe form of conjunctivitis that also affects the cornea underneath. Signs of conjunctivitis include pink eye (Fig. 14.20) with thick mucus, pain, and difficulty opening the eyes after sleeping (due to dried mucus). Infection of the conjunctiva by some bacteria, fungi (e.g., Candida sp., Aspergillus sp.), protozoan parasites (e.g., Acanthamoeba sp. from contaminated contact lenses), and herpes simplex virus-1 can lead to ulceration and subsequent keratitis. Untreated ulcerative eye diseases and keratitis may result in blindness and brain involvement. These diseases are detected through eye examinations and microbe-specific tests. For example, herpetic keratitis is detected by the branching (dendritic) lesion on the eye and PCR tests. The diseases are treated with oral and topical antiviral drugs such as ganciclovir and valacyclovir. Keratoplasty (corneal transplant) may be necessary if damage is extensive. Healthcare professionals should use protective eye coverings to reduce the risk of eye infection. Many infections occur through the eye as a portal of entry, especially viral ones, and may not cause symptoms in the eyes but can cause respiratory and systemic infections. About 3-6 million cases of conjunctivitis and about 60,000 cases of keratitis occur in the USA annually, of which over 70% are due to viral infections.

Trachoma is a keratoconjunctivitis caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis. The bacteria infect the inner surfaces of the eyelids, leading to tissue hardening. This hardened tissue rubbing against the cornea causes inflammation. If left untreated, the disease worsens, leading to eyelid deformity and eyelashes rubbing against the conjunctiva (Fig. 14.20). The cornea becomes inflamed and scarred, eventually becoming opaque. An ophthalmologist can detect the infection by eye examination. Early infections can be treated with azithromycin. More advanced infections may also require surgical correction of the eyelid. Globally, about 40 million people, mostly children in Africa, have trachoma, with approximately 2 million blinded by the disease. Trachoma generally does not transmit sexually; it is transmitted by direct contact in crowded living conditions. Although around 1.6 million cases of sexually transmitted Chlamydia trachomatis are reported annually in the United States, trachoma is extremely rare in the USA. Cough Cough is a reflex that can be voluntary or involuntary, involving a deep inhalation followed by a forced exhalation. It is triggered by the brain's cough center to clear mucus and solid particles from the airways. Various infections of the upper or lower respiratory tract can increase cough frequency. A productive cough expels mucus, which can be bloody, while a dry cough produces no mucus. A cough that lasts more than three weeks is considered subacute, and one lasting longer than eight weeks is classified as chronic. Patients with subacute or chronic cough should seek medical attention to determine the underlying cause and receive appropriate treatment.
Croup

It is a childhood illness caused by viral infections, especially parainfluenza virus, characterized by inflammation of the trachea and larynx, and marked by a barking (hoarse) cough. Affected children may also have a fever, runny nose, and sore throat. The symptoms worsen at night and may include difficulty breathing and swallowing. Croup is detected by physical examination and is treated supportively, with nebulizers and steroids (to open the airways), cough suppressants, and ventilation if necessary.
Fibrosis of the lung

Fibrosis (scarring) in the lungs can occur after lung recovery from pneumonia or severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Inflammation in severely damaged lung tissue, including damage to the alveolar epithelium, activates lung myofibroblasts to secrete excessive collagen fibers. The scar results from improper healing of the lung involving excess fibrous (scar) tissue. Lung infections caused by many microbes, including SARS-CoV, influenza, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, HCV, Staphylococcus aureus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Propionibacterium acnes, and Pneumocystis jirovecii infection, may trigger lung fibrosis. Symptoms of the disease include persistent dry cough, shortness of breath, and fatigue. The disease is detected by physical examination and computed tomography (CT) scan (Fig. 14.20). The disease cannot be fully treated (the damage is irreversible) but can be managed to prevent further progression through supportive therapy.
Fungal ball

It is a form of mycetoma characterized by the noninvasive buildup of fungal hyphae in body cavities, especially the maxillary sinuses and lungs, primarily due to Aspergillus sp. infections (Fig. 14.21). The disease can be asymptomatic (in about 10% of cases) or present with symptoms such as yellow or greenish sputum, pressure on the jaw and eyeballs, and headaches. The condition can be diagnosed through microscopic examination of sputum, nasal endoscopy, and CT scans. Symptomatic cases are treated with surgery and postoperative therapies.
Influenza

It is a spectrum of diseases caused by human influenza viruses A, B, and C, as well as some zoonotic influenza viruses, especially those from birds and swine. Symptoms include high fever, sore throat, runny nose, cough, pneumonia, severe body and muscle pain, secondary bacterial infection of the lungs, a cytokine storm, and sepsis. The severity of the signs varies depending on the virus species and strain. The incubation period after contact is about 1-4 days, and symptoms last for about a week. The disease may cause mortality by leading to ARDS, pneumonia, cardiovascular complications, and encephalitis. Influenza is detected through signs of illness and RT-PCR testing using RNA extracted from a nasal swab. Treatment includes supportive therapy (rest, hydration, and fever management with non- aspirin drugs), while complicated cases and debilitated patients are treated with antiviral agents such as oseltamivir and zanamivir.

With a multi-fragmented RNA genome and an error-prone RNA polymerase, influenza viruses are among the fastest- mutating viruses known, with many new strains emerging each year. Occasionally, avian and swine viruses are transmitted to humans, leading to antigenic shifts. An annual vaccine is recommended for vulnerable groups, such as children, adults aged 65 and older, and those with weakened immune systems. Despite these efforts, about 50 million flu cases occur each year in the United States, resulting in over 40,000 deaths. Vaccinated individuals are not completely protected but generally experience milder illness. Global pandemics caused by specific strains of influenza A have occurred in 1918-20, 1957-58, and 1968-69, killing an estimated 100 million, 1-2 million, and 1-4 million people, respectively. Influenza remains a constant occupational hazard for healthcare workers. Proper and frequent handwashing, wearing and regularly cleaning appropriate garments, annual vaccination, and the use of face masks can help reduce the risk of influenza infection. The economic burden of influenza in the United States is about $29 billion. Metastatic hydatid cysts in the lung It is a rare hydatid cyst disease caused by the larvae of Echinococcus multilocularis. It primarily develops in the liver and the lungs. Unlike typical hydatid cysts (caused by the larvae of E. granulosus), metastatic hydatid cysts are not fluid-filled pressure chambers; they lack a capsule and grow like metastatic tumors. The disease is endemic in the northern hemisphere, including China, Siberia, Central Europe, and North America, where about 10,000 cases are reported annually. The disease is detected by a CT scan (Fig. 14.21) and treated by surgery and albendazole. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) It is categorized as a head and neck cancer and is associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection. The virus persistently (latently) infects B lymphocytes in people exposed to it or who have survived infectious mononucleosis. However, NPC is a cancer of epithelial cells (not a B cell cancer). The disease symptoms include painless lumps in the neck, nose bleeding, and facial pain (Fig. 14.21). The disease is diagnosed by physical examination, needle biopsy of the lump, CT scan, and history of EBV infection. The disease is treated with chemo/radiotherapy and immunochemotherapy. The disease is endemic in South-East Asia, Southern China, and North Africa, where about 120,000 cases are reported every year.

Ocular larva migrans (toxocariasis and loiasis) Accidental ingestion of cat or dog feces contaminated with eggs of the nematode worms of the genus Toxocara initiates toxocariasis. The egg hatches in the intestine, and the larvae penetrate the intestinal wall and enter the bloodstream. African eyeworm (Loa loa) larvae enter the human body through the bite of a deerfly. The larvae can migrate to various parts of the body, causing different signs of disease (for example, meningitis if they migrate to the brain). The larva may migrate to the eye, causing signs such as vision loss, misalignment, white spots in the pupil, and inflammation (Fig. 14.22). The disease can be diagnosed through an eye examination and a blood test (to check for an elevated eosinophil count). The disease is treated with albendazole (for toxocariasis) and diethylcarbamazine (for loiasis), if needed, along with supportive therapy such as corticosteroids to suppress inflammation. With approximately 150 million cats and dogs, toxocariasis is quite common in the United States. About 10% of the population is seropositive for the parasite, although the number of reported cases of ocular larva migrans remains negligible. About 15 million people in central and western Africa are infected with L. loa. Travelers from other parts of the world (including the United States) to this endemic range of the worm occasionally are diagnosed with the disease.

Otitis externa and otitis media

Outer ear infections (otitis externa, or swimmer's ear) are primarily caused by Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. External ear injury and moisture in the ear canal help initiate infections. The disease signs include pain, swelling, and drainage from open wounds (Fig. 14.22). Middle ear infection (otitis media) begins when oral microbes (including about 60 bacterial species, such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis, as well as some viruses that cause the common cold) enter the middle ear via the Eustachian tube. Inflammation following the infection closes the Eustachian canal, creating an anaerobic environment where some bacteria grow rapidly and release gases. Accumulated gases can cause painful pressure and rupture the eardrum. Bottle-fed children are among the most vulnerable groups to otitis media.

An ear infection can be diagnosed based on the patient’s history and an ear examination with an otoscope (Fig. 14.22). Some ear infections resolve spontaneously and can be cared for with pain management; however, bacterial infections may require oral antibiotic therapy. A ruptured eardrum usually heals after the infection is controlled. Some children develop recurrent otitis media, requiring an ear tube to be inserted into the eardrum.

Otitis is extremely common in the United States. The incidence rates for otitis externa and media are 123 and 60.5 per 1000 people. Children aged 5-12 years are most vulnerable to otitis externa, and those aged 6-24 months are more prone to otitis media. Proper swimming training may reduce the risk of otitis externa, while breastfeeding and feeding infants and children in a sitting position (and not lying on the bed) may reduce the risk of otitis media. Pneumonia and pneumonitis Pneumonia is an inflammation of the alveoli that causes fluid buildup and impairs gas exchange. Pneumonitis is inflammation of the alveoli (pneumonia-like symptoms) due to noninfectious factors. It can occur due to inhalation of dust, mold, type I hypersensitivity reactions, and radiation therapy. The typical symptoms of pneumonia are caused by bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Hemophilus influenzae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and S. agalactiae. Yersinia pestis causes pneumonic plague, pneumonia with sudden high fever, chest pain, and shortness of breath. Mycobacterium tuberculosis and M. avium complex, and the fungus Pneumocystis jirovecii may also cause pneumonia among debilitated patients. These symptoms include fever, a productive cough, shortness of breath, chest pain, and severe fatigue. The severity of the disease depends on how much lung tissue is affected. Patients can transmit the disease agent via aerosols and thus require isolation. Diagnosis can be made through physical examination, chest X-ray, and blood tests. Pneumonia is usually treated with antibiotics. Patients also need rest and supportive care, such as hydration, ventilation if needed, and fever control. Patients who recover, particularly those infected with K. pneumoniae, may experience lasting lung damage.

Pneumonia caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydophila pneumoniae, Legionella pneumophila, some fungi, and some viruses (including respiratory syncytial virus, influenza virus, and some strains of coronaviruses) is called atypical pneumonia, because the disease shows less severe symptoms, such as low-grade fever, non-productive cough, headache, and less accumulation of fluid in the lung. Diagnosis and treatment of the disease are the same as those for typical pneumonia. Note that incapacitated patients may develop pneumonia from saliva flooding the lungs. Pneumonia is common in the United States, with about 1.5 million cases each year and roughly 50,000 deaths. Childhood pneumonia has been significantly reduced in the USA because of the effective vaccines for S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae. At present, elderly people (65 or older) are the most vulnerable group.
Respiratory anthrax

Inhalation of Bacillus anthracis endospores is necessary for the disease to develop. The endospores germinate in the lung, and the resulting vegetative bacteria secrete exotoxins. The exotoxins LTx and ETx cause pneumonia by activating adenyl cyclase and raising cAMP levels in lung epithelial cells. Symptoms include fever, cough, shortness of breath, and shock. The mortality rate can be up to 85%, mainly due to delays in diagnosis and treatment. The disease can be treated with antibiotics like doxycycline or levofloxacin and supportive care. People involved in farming, wool processing, and handling animal bones are at higher risk of respiratory anthrax. B. anthracis endospore has been weaponized by several countries and has been used in bioterrorism in the USA and Japan. An effective vaccine is available but is only administered to special individuals.
Retinitis

Retinitis caused by infections involves inflammation of the retina due to viruses (such as cytomegalovirus, Fig. 14.23), bacteria (such as Borrelia sp.), and parasites (such as Toxoplasma gondii). Signs of the disease include patients experiencing light flashes, blurred vision, and vision loss, especially at night. The condition is usually diagnosed based on symptoms and eye examination and treated with antimicrobial agents and supportive therapies (such as vitamin A therapy, anti-inflammatory treatment, and eyeglasses).
Scarlet fever

The disease is caused by the erythrogenic toxin of Streptococcus pyogenes and is characterized by pink skin (Fig. 14.23). Affected individuals (mostly children 5-15 years) also experience sore throat, inflamed tongue (strawberry tongue), fever, and body aches. Scarlett fever is diagnosed based on clinical signs and a throat culture and is treated with oral antibiotics. If left untreated, it can lead to severe complications such as throat abscess and rheumatic fever (involving joint and heart diseases). S. pyogenes infection kills about 500,000 people globally. About 15-30% of the children in the USA get S. pyogenes infection every year.

Sinusitis

Sinusitis is inflammation of the nasal sinuses caused by viral (usually rhinovirus, parainfluenza virus, or influenza virus), or bacterial (mainly Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, or Moraxella catarrhalis) infections. Allergies are also associated with sinusitis. Infection-related sinusitis involves closing the sinus tubes. The symptoms include nasal and forehead pain, pressure, nasal congestion, headache, postnasal drip, gum pain, bad breath, sore throat, and fever. The disease is diagnosed based on symptoms, nasal endoscopy, and CT scan (Fig. 14.23), and treated with nasal corticosteroids and decongestants. Antibiotics are used if a bacterial infection is involved or if the symptoms last longer than ten days. The condition is considered chronic if it lingers for more than 12 weeks and repeats frequently. Sinusitis is a major public health problem in the United States, affecting 12% of the population annually, costing some $12 billion dollars, including about $3 billion in direct drug costs.

Tonsillitis, pharyngitis, laryngitis, and epiglottitis These diseases are inflammation of the throat (pharynx), the voice box (larynx), and the epiglottis, respectively (Fig. 14.23), caused mainly by viruses (mainly adenovirus, rhinovirus, influenza virus, or coronaviruses) and a few bacterial species, particularly Streptococcus pyogenes. The signs of tonsillitis, pharyngitis, and epiglottitis include redness, swelling of the tonsils, and painful swallowing. The signs of laryngitis include a drastic change in the voice (hoarseness) and a temporary inability to vocalize. Additional signs include fever, swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck, pink eye, breathing difficulties, and cough. The conditions are diagnosed by physical examination and throat culture. Since most cases are viral infections, treatment includes rest and supportive therapy. Breathing difficulty requires ventilation. To rule out bacterial (Streptococcal) infection, a blood agar plate culture is performed, and the positive cases are treated with appropriate antibiotics. An untreated bacterial sore throat can lead to severe complications, such as scarlet fever, sepsis, and rheumatic fever. Children with repeated tonsillitis may require tonsillectomy. Pharyngitis accounts for 1-2% of doctors’ office visits in the United States. Children under 15 years old are among the most vulnerable group. Children having a full range of routine vaccinations are less prone to these diseases.
Tuberculosis

The disease, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, may affect various tissues, but the lung is the primary target, where the bacterium causes granuloma. About 5% of the patients who contract the germ develop clinical tuberculosis (TB) within two years, showing signs such as night sweats, fever, weight loss, fatigue, body pain, and coughing that yields sputum with pus and blood. About 90% of the patients develop latent TB (LTBI), showing no disease signs for many years. Active TB may develop later in life in many patients with LTBI, particularly patients with immunosuppression. Patients with poor cell-mediated immunity may develop disseminated TB affecting multiple organs, including the skin and brain. On the other hand, heavily infected patients with good cell-mediated immunity may develop autoimmune diseases such as arthritis, vasculitis, and erythema. TB is detected by microscopic examination of sputum, PCR of DNA extracted from sputum, and chest X-ray (Fig. 14.24). The tuberculin skin test can also be used, but positive test results do not indicate whether the patient has active TB; rather, they indicate that the subject had TB in the past or has LTBI.

TB is treated with combination antibiotic therapy for about six months. TB that responds to the first-line antibiotics (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) is drug-sensitive TB (DS-TB, see Fig. 14.24). TB resistant to one of these drugs is considered drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). Multidrug-resistant TB (MDR TB) is resistant to isoniazid and rifampin, and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR TB) is resistant to isoniazid and rifampin, fluoroquinolone, and at least one of the three injectable second-line drugs (i.e., amikacin, kanamycin, or capreomycin). Patients with such a disease are isolated and treated with antibiotics after conducting an antibiogram. These antibiotics are toxic, and many patients cannot tolerate them and become non-compliant. For them, direct observation therapy is administered, where a person witnesses the patient taking the pills. TB is one of the most severe global public health problems, with about 25% of the population infected, 11 million new cases, and 1.2 million deaths every year. TB is less common (about 10,000 new cases per year) in the United States.
Whooping cough

It is a contagious, mostly childhood disease caused by Bordetella pertussis and some related species that produce pertussis toxin (a type III exotoxin). The pathogens enter the lungs, destroy the cilia of epithelial cells, and then release the exotoxin. The disease signs during the first couple of weeks include cold-like symptoms followed by the paroxysmal stage. During this stage, the A subunit of the A-B5-type toxin (ultimately) activates adenylyl cyclase in epithelial cells, leading to excessive, thick mucus secretion. The bacterium also causes an excessive accumulation of leukocytes in the airways. The thick mucus triggers violent coughing that expels all air from the lungs and may last up to 2 minutes per episode (paroxysms) for several weeks (Fig. 14.24). During paroxysms, children cannot breathe, which reduces oxygen levels in the brain. After the ~2-minute paroxysms, the child struggles to rapidly inhale, which makes a whopping (loud gasping) noise, giving the name of the disease. Repeated coughing, especially at night, can make children get exhausted and may cause seizures, brain damage, and death. The disease can be detected from disease signs and PCR of DNA extracted from a nasal swab, and treated with common antibiotics (erythromycin, etc.). Antibodies to neutralize the pertussis toxin in the affected patients have yet to be developed. Since the disease is caused by an exotoxin rather than the bacterium, early treatment prevents the development of damaging disease signs. The highly effective vaccine (DTaP and Tdap) has reduced whooping cough to about a million cases globally (including 35,000 in the USA), but recently the number of cases has been on the upswing. Recently, older children and elderly people have been getting whooping cough, because the whooping cough vaccine does not provide lifelong immunity. Although infection in older people is less damaging, they are advised to receive the vaccine.
